subject: Maths
central_question: How can algebraic identities be visualised, proved, and used to expand, factorise, simplify, and solve mathematical expressions efficiently?
in_scope_units: 4.1 Introduction — recognising numerical patterns and using algebra to explain why they always hold.
4.2 Visualising Identities — distinguishing identities from equations and deriving (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² through area models and distributivity.
4.3 Factorisation of Algebraic Expressions Using Identities — recognising perfect-square forms, taking common factors, deriving (a − b)², and using identities for quick calculations.
4.4 More Identities — developing (a + b + c)², revisiting a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), and applying identities to numerical squares and algebraic factorisation.
4.5 Factorisation Using Algebra Tiles — representing products and quadratic factorisation through rectangular arrangements of x²-tiles, x-tiles, and unit tiles.
4.6 Factorisation Without Using Algebra Tiles — splitting the middle term by finding numbers with the required sum and product, including positive and negative cases.
4.7 Finding New Identities — deriving cube identities, sum and difference of cubes, and x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz through distributivity and geometric models.
4.8 Simplifying Rational Expressions — factorising numerator and denominator, cancelling only non-zero common factors, and applying factorisation to geometric and real-life problems.
banned_topics: General solution of quadratic equations by the quadratic formula
Graphs of quadratic polynomials and parabolas
Remainder theorem and factor theorem as separate polynomial theorems
Advanced binomial theorem for arbitrary powers

known_pitfalls.claim: An identity is just any equation containing variables.
known_pitfalls.correction: An algebraic identity is an equation that is true for all allowed values of its variables; an ordinary equation may be true only for particular values.
The correct identity is (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; the middle term 2ab comes from the two rectangles in the area model.
The correct identity is (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², while a² − b² factorises as (a + b)(a − b).

known_pitfalls.claim: Any two factors of the constant term can be used when factorising x² + bx + c.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chosen numbers must have product c and sum b; both conditions must be satisfied at the same time.

known_pitfalls.claim: In a perfect-square trinomial, matching the first and last square terms is enough.
known_pitfalls.correction: The middle term must also equal +2ab or −2ab, depending on whether the factor is (a + b)² or (a − b)².

known_pitfalls.claim: A common term may be cancelled directly from a sum in a rational expression.
known_pitfalls.correction: Only common factors of the entire numerator and denominator may be cancelled, and the cancelled factor must be non-zero.

known_pitfalls.claim: The signs in (a − b)³ are all negative after the first term.
known_pitfalls.correction: The signs alternate: (a − b)³ = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³.

known_pitfalls.claim: The identity x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz can always be simplified to zero.
known_pitfalls.correction: It equals (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − xz − yz), so it is zero only when one of these factors is zero.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with Textbook Example 1: test three consecutive square numbers and then prove algebraically why the result is always 2.
Use Textbook Examples 2–4 and Exercise Set 4.1 Q1(i): verify and apply (a + b)² with negative numbers, rational numbers, algebraic terms, and 43².
Continue with Textbook Examples 5–8 and Exercise Set 4.2 Q1(i): recognise perfect-square trinomials, take a common factor, derive (a − b)², and evaluate 29².
Use Textbook Example 9 and Exercise Set 4.3 Q3(i): expand a three-term square and connect the algebra to the geometric model in Fig. 4.4.
Use Textbook Examples 10–12 and Exercise Set 4.4 Q1(i): factor quadratics by matching the sum and product needed for the split middle term.
Use Textbook Examples 13–15: recognise cube identities and apply x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz to a structured numerical problem.
Finish with Textbook Examples 16–18 and Exercise Set 4.5 Q1(vi): simplify rational expressions under denominator restrictions and apply factorisation to dimensions and area.
